newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom denies keeping Kirch at bay.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom denies keeping Kirch at bay.

text.p: Deutsche Telekom AG on Thursday denied charges that it has been stalling in talks with the Kirch Group over putting its DF1 digital pay television channel on Telekom's cable TV network.
Kirch Group officials have said recently that Telekom was blocking access to the cable network for their DF1 digital pay television channel, which is now only available over satellite.
"Such statements are nonsense," Telekom chairman Ron Sommer told a group of foreign journalists in Bonn.
"We are involved in very reasonable negotiations and are looking for a business-like solution. That is what this is about, a business-like resolution, how to split the proceeds."

Telekom has a monopoly over the trunk cable TV network in Germany, which connects some 16 million homes. There is competition at the local level because local cable TV companies are allowed to connect customers to the trunk network.

As a result, Telekom only has 5.6 million of the total cable TV subscribers under direct contract. The rest are under contract to alternative providers. The largest of these is Vebacom, which has some 1.2 million subscribers.
Telekom wants to revamp the way it charges broadcasters for access to the cable TV network.

In the past it has charged a transmission fee that was so low it did not even cover operating costs. Contrary to international practice, cable operators have not shared any of the revenues generated by the broadcasters.
But that will all change. Telekom is in talks with other cable TV operators and German media regulators about changing the way it bills broadcasters.

Telekom officials have indicated that the company would like to cut or even scrap the transmission fee and instead pay broadcasters a fee per subscriber. It would take a share of advertising and pay TV subscriber revenues in exchange.
Partly because of a lack of capacity in the cable telvision network, media regulators have decided which programmes would be carried. But that is also under discusssion.

Telekom, other cable TV operators and regulators are trying to draw up a so-called "must carry" list, which would set out which broadcasters would be required, leaving the operators themselves to decide about the rest.
The changes have given rise to speculation that Telekom wants to begin amassing film rights.
"We do not want to get into the content business," Sommer said. "We want to cooperate with content providers, but not for free."
By the end of this year there will be 31 cable channels based on the analogue PAL standard and up to 150 digital channels, ending the squeeze in the cable network.
The change will mark a huge shift in the German cable television market and allow for the launch of digital pay television networks like Kirch's DF1.

Kirch and Telekom have been talking about the conditions of inclusion in the cable network of DF1, which is now only available over satellite. They are also talking about the basic decoder technology for digital pay TV.
Telekom has said it would decide on which decoder standard it would use early next year.
